children: 1111 ET - With U.S. diesel prices hitting new all-time highs above $6 a gallon, "many independent truckers are likely being forced to sideline rigs temporarily until prices drop back down to around $4 or below," Ritterbusch & Associates says in a note. That's even with some ability to pass on the increased costs to final goods, which bodes ill for inflation down the road, the firm says. "Diesel will remain as the strongest part of the energy complex as long as Hormuz remains clogged." The AAA reports the average U.S. diesel price at a record $6.0556 a gallon. Nymex diesel futures are off 0.7% at $5.0265 a gallon while WTI crude retreats 2.9% after an eight-session rally. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1056 ET - Palantir's pitch about the importance of AI and data sovereignty is sinking in, D.A. Davidson analysts Gil Luria and Turner Dischinger say in a note, raising their price target by $50 to $250. Nvidia's partnership with Palantir, announced Thursday, reinforces the trust major enterprises place in the company--especially as OpenAI and Anthropic "keep getting caught with their hand in the cookie jar" with "comically false" claims that they don't look at customer data, the analysts say. "Customers are getting savvier about what AI model they need and how to work with a range of models and Palantir is capitalizing on that trend," Luria and Dischinger say. "Trust means Palantir is naturally positioned to become the control plane, orchestration layer and harness provider for a wide range of customers."  (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1034 ET - The markets now expect the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points next week, but the impact of the hike may be muted, LPL Financial's Jeffrey Roach says in a note. A widening share of economic activity is less sensitive to interest rates, similar to what was seen during the Fed's hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023, the economist says. Demand could remain resilient despite a tighter policy due to surging AI investment and continued spending on travel from affluent consumers, Roach says. He expects nominal economic growth will remain higher than 6% in the coming quarters. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1021 ET - Investors may have overlooked Oracle management's focus on its AI Data Platform, a layer in which artificial-intelligence systems can operate using proprietary enterprise data. The company's commentary, though, underlines what StoneX analyst Yi Fu Lee sees as the centrality of data for enterprise AI adoption. Both Oracle and Snowflake are now "effectively arguing AI models matter, but proprietary enterprise data determines who captures long-term value," Lee writes. "This continues to support our view that data infrastructure remains one of the most attractive layers of the AI stack." The Oracle first-quarter report implies positive read-throughs for Snowflake, MongoDB, and the private company Databricks. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1011 ET - Oracle's F1Q report should help build confidence that its data-center buildout is going as planned and will be converted into revenue, JPMorgan says in a note. The company told investors that its incremental $30 billion of AI contracts probably won't demand more cash outlays beyond its prior guidance for $40 billion of capital in the current fiscal year, according to the analysts. The company also forecast that around half of its $664 billion in remaining performance obligations will convert to revenue in the next three years, and appears to have made progress on diversifying its data-center buildout, reducing the risk from any single project being delayed, the analysts say. Investors may still question whether Oracle's cash outlay will moderate significantly after FY28, particularly with the robust industry demand backdrop, the analysts add. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1003 ET - Disney's subscription video on demand business is prioritizing revenue after achieving sustainable profitability, Benchmark analyst Mike Hickey says. The media conglomerate had 13% margins for subscription video on demand in the fiscal third quarter, and management doesn't expect margins to retreat materially or fall below a double-digit percentage, Hickey says. "This represents an incremental shift from providing profitability toward reinvesting to accelerate growth," Hickey says. Life-sports advertising demand also remains strong, while AI, healthcare and political advertising business are performing well. (katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

0955 ET - Oracle's compute capacity for the rest of the year doesn't depend on the company battling through delays and opposition for certain of its flagship data-center projects, KeyBanc Capital Markets analysts write in a note. The company's disclosure that it brought 850 megawatts of capacity online during the first quarter "could not have been better timed with concerns over data center pushback from some key states where Oracle has GW+ sized projects," the analysts write. "The sum of the other projects in flight is able to offset any delays that may be happening and with the increased revenue guidance management clearly feels the capacity roadmap is enough to deliver on its revenue targets this year." (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

0954 ET - Descartes Systems is turning AI from an investor question mark to a key growth engine. TD Cowen's John Shao says the logistics software company has "made meaningful progress in productizing AI," where its "strategy and readiness... could have a more significant and potentially strategic impact on the company's long-term growth and profitability." The analyst says that this is a leap from where the company was a year ago, when the company would respond to investor concerns over AI. Now, Shao says management is proactive with its strategy, with a "tangible roadmap spanning AI infrastructure, connectivity, product design, and specific use cases across the company's major business lines." (adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

0946 ET - The U.S. 2-year yield is sensitive to expectations for short-term interest rates. The core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices came in hotter than analysts expected in August, rising 0.3% month-over-month versus the expectation of 0.2%. The U.S. 2-year yield rose to 4.598%. Odds for a rate hike at next week's Fed meeting also climbed to nearly 90%. A month ago, those odds were nearly split.(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

0945 ET - The August CPI showing inflation rising 3.4% year-over-year, and the core up 2.4%, strengthens the case for a Fed rate hike next week says to Karl Schamotta, Chief Market Strategist at Corpay in a note. "In our view, the balance of risks facing the Fed now favors raising rates. With core price growth showing signs of accelerating, oil benchmarks up more than 78% this year, tariffs rising once again, Washington floating fiscal giveaways, and artificial intelligence investment still flowing, there's little to suggest that inflation pressures are set to ease in the months ahead, giving officials little choice but to take action now." Futures traders seem to agree with the CME's FedWatch Tool now showing an 85% likelihood that the Fed will raise rates by a quarter-point. (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

0941 ET - Kroger says shoppers are prioritizing higher-quality food, despite pressures on their budgets. Engagement has been strong with Kroger's natural and organic products, executives say on a call with analysts. The company added more than 600 new natural and organic items to meet this growing demand, they say. The trend comes as customers are putting fewer items in their baskets and grocery unit growth has slowed down. Executives say consumers are feeling pressured by higher gas prices and other economic conditions that are limiting their grocery budgets.(katherine.hamilton@wsj.com)

0930 ET - Now that economists have the PPI and CPI print in hand, they can start calculating their forecasts for PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Capital Economics now estimates the PCE deflator rose by 0.27% month-over-month in August. Some economists estimated that upcoming methodological changes at the BEA, which publishes PCE, could relieve some pressure on the core PCE deflator. But, Capital's Stephen Brown says that projection is unlikely to be affected much by the revisions to portfolio management and software & accessories price calculations. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)
